title: Eclipse Glasses Sold Out? Here's How to Watch Safely Without Them
summary: It's the most significant solar eclipse in the UK since 1999, and everyone's talking about it. But there's a problem: eclipse glasses are sold out everywhere. Online orders won't arrive in time. So what's a curious sky-watcher to do? Don't worry — you can still witness this once-in-a-generation spectacle using items you probably have in your kitchen. On Wednesday evening, the UK will experience a partial eclipse, where the Moon covers part of the Sun. (Parts of Spain, Greenland, and Iceland will see a total eclipse.) But experts warn: never look directly at the Sun without special glasses. Regular sunglasses or dark goggles won't protect your eyes — they don't block enough UV radiation, and you could permanently damage your vision, according to The Royal Astronomical Society. So here's a cool trick: make a pinhole projector. Take a piece of card and poke a small hole in the center with a ballpoint pen tip. Hold the card in one hand and a blank piece of paper in the other, with your back to the Sun. Line them up so the Sun's image projects onto the paper. You'll see a miniature version of the eclipse! Or use a colander — the kitchen strainer. Eye specialist David Jones, a consultant ophthalmologist at Royal Cornwall Hospitals Trust, says it's his favorite method. "If you hold the colander to the Sun and you look away from the Sun, protecting your eyes, you can make not just one picture of the Sun but a hundred all at once," he demonstrated in a social media video. So grab a colander or craft a pinhole viewer, and enjoy the show safely. Your eyes will thank you!
why_it_matters: This story shows how scientific knowledge can reduce a serious health risk during a rare shared event: understanding how to observe indirectly lets people take part without damaging their eyesight, even when safety equipment runs out.

keywords.explanation: A partial eclipse happens when the Moon covers only part of the Sun from where you are watching.
A total eclipse happens when the Moon completely blocks the Sun for viewers in a certain area.
UV radiation is invisible solar energy that can burn and damage your eyes.
A pinhole projector is a simple device that lets you see the Sun indirectly through a tiny hole.
An ophthalmologist is a doctor who specializes in eye health and vision.
This is the public health organization that runs hospitals in Cornwall, England.

background_read: The last time UK sky-watchers saw a solar eclipse this significant was in 1999, when a total eclipse was visible from Cornwall and parts of Devon.
Unlike a total eclipse, a partial eclipse never darkens the sky enough to make the Sun safe to view without protection.
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes directly between Earth and the Sun, blocking some or all of the Sun's light; a partial eclipse means only part of the Sun is covered.

The Royal Astronomical Society (a British scientific society founded in 1820 that promotes astronomy) warns that even when the Sun is partly covered, its UV radiation can burn the retina and cause permanent eye damage.

David Jones, the consultant ophthalmologist at Royal Cornwall Hospitals Trust (an NHS hospital trust in southwest England), has used social media to show the colander method because it creates many safe images at once.

perspectives.description: Educators and curious families see the pinhole projector and colander method as an inventive, low-cost way to join a rare event without specialist equipment. They argue that sold-out glasses do not have to exclude anyone from experiencing the eclipse safely.

Ophthalmologists and public health campaigners worry that some people will still glance directly at the Sun or use regular sunglasses, risking permanent retinal damage. They stress that even a partial eclipse covers only part of the Sun, so the remaining visible crescent is still dangerous.

Astronomers note that the UK is seeing only a partial eclipse, not totality, and that its significance comes largely from being the most substantial UK eclipse since 1999. From an observational standpoint, the event is a chance to explain how the Moon's shadow creates partial and total eclipses.

After this eclipse, the practical lesson about pinhole viewers may help more people prepare for future eclipses. Public science groups hope the colander trick and simple demonstrations will become standard safety advice for the next major celestial event.
